about: Learn's three guides. Rows marked app describe what Dialed In does, not facts about coffee, and carry no source.

guides.name: From cherry to cup
guides.teaser: Where your coffee was before the bag · 3 min
guides.lede: Every bag went through the same few stages before it reached you. Each one can change the cup.

steps.title: It starts as a fruit
steps.text: Coffee beans are the seeds of a fruit called a cherry. Arabica, the species most specialty coffee comes from, is a natural cross of two other coffee species that formed in Ethiopia's forests.

steps.title: The variety is the kind of tree
steps.text: Like apples, coffee comes in varieties: Caturra, SL28, Gesha. Names on bags aren't always right, though: in one DNA study, only 39% of coffees sold as Gesha matched it.

steps.title: Where it grows
steps.text: In a study on Réunion island, the air temperature while the beans developed strongly shaped the cup: cooler farms gave more acidity and fruit.

steps.title: Processing takes the fruit off
steps.text: Washed coffees have the fruit removed before drying; naturals dry inside it; honeys are in between. In an Ethiopian trial of seven varieties at three sites, where it was grown and how it was processed both affected cup scores, alongside the variety.

steps.title: Resting and shipping
steps.text: Dried coffee usually rests 30 to 60 days where it was grown, is milled out of its papery parchment, and then spends about six weeks at sea.

steps.title: Roasting
steps.text: The roaster turns the green seeds brown. Roasters name their roast levels differently, so one roaster's light may be another's medium.

steps.title: Resting after the roast
steps.text: Many roasters suggest letting beans rest about 5 to 14 days for filter and 7 to 14 for espresso. That's their rule of thumb, not settled science.
steps.label: anecdotal

steps.title: Your cup
steps.text: Then it's yours: dose, grind, water and time. In one study, changing only how strong it was brewed and how much was extracted moved the same coffee between sour, bitter and sweet.

guides.name: How to read a coffee bag
guides.teaser: Every word, from SL28 to AA · 4 min
guides.lede: Every line on a specialty bag tells you something about the cup. Tap a number to see what it means; one opens at a time.

bag.name: Nyeri AA
bag.note: A made-up bag, written the way real ones are.

rows.title: Origin: Nyeri, Kenya
rows.text: Nyeri is one of Kenya's main coffee counties, with farms around 1,600–2,000 m. A county or region tells you more than the country alone.

rows.title: Variety: SL28, SL34
rows.text: Two trees picked at Scott Labs in Kenya in the 1930s. Not one family: by DNA, SL28 is Bourbon-like and SL34 Typica-like.

rows.title: Process: washed, double fermented
rows.text: Washed, then soaked under clean water before drying, Kenya's classic way. Since the fruit is already off, the soak “isn't so much a fermentation”, as one coffee researcher put it.

rows.title: Grade: AA
rows.text: AA means the biggest beans of the usual Kenyan grades. It's a size, not a taste score.

rows.title: Altitude: 1,700–1,900 m
rows.text: About 5,600–6,200 ft. Near the equator, higher farms are cooler, and in one study cooler farms gave more acidity and fruit.

rows.title: Notes: blackcurrant, grapefruit
rows.text: Tasting notes describe what the roaster tasted; they don't mean flavor was added. Coffees co-fermented or infused with fruit or spice are different, and not all are clearly labeled. Your cup may differ: brewing alone can move the same coffee a long way.

guides.name: Washed vs natural, side by side
guides.teaser: A tasting you can do this week · 2 bags
guides.lede: The quickest way to learn what processing does: taste the same kind of coffee both ways, back to back.

steps.title: Find two bags
steps.text: A washed and a natural from the same country, ideally from the same roaster. Ethiopia is a good place to look: both styles are common there.

steps.title: Brew them the same way
steps.text: Same dose, ratio, water and grind setting for both, so the process is the main difference.

steps.title: Taste the washed first
steps.text: Washed coffees are usually clean, bright and crisp, with more acidity.

steps.title: Then the natural
steps.text: Look for berry, stone fruit or dried fruit and a heavier body. A wine-like or boozy note is the natural process too.

steps.title: Which did you like?
steps.text: Your taste decides. In one trial of 11 varieties, washed scored the same or higher every time, though for some the gap was under a point.

steps.title: Log both, then compare
steps.text: Log each one, then open Compare on either coffee to see the two flavor shapes on top of each other.
